newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus agree to push for union.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus agree to push for union.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Belarus leader Alexander Lukashenko agreed on Friday to push for closer union between their two Slav states and reiterated their common hostility towards NATO's eastward expansion plans.
Yeltsin, who looked energetic and fit, welcomed the hardline Belarus president in the Kremlin, saying Moscow was committed to seeking stronger ties with its western neighbour.
"Commonwealth with Belarus is the common desire of our peoples and we will not deviate from this path," said Yeltsin, kissing Lukashenko on the cheek.
The two leaders signed a joint declaration that called for integration of their countries' customs, fiscal, transport and energy systems and synchronisation of economic reforms.
The declaration also touched on the sensitive issue of NATO's plans to admit several former Warsaw Pact countries, probably including Belarus's neighbour Poland, later this year.
"Our countries are united in their non-acceptance of NATO's plans for eastward expansion, which will create new lines of division in Europe and dangerous confrontation," it said.

Yeltsin and Lukashenko signed a pact in April 1996 forming an economic "community" but there has been little concrete progress in furthering integration, partly due to the Russian president's long illnesses from which he is only just emerging.
Lukashenko said later that despite the common desire for unity, their future marriage cannot be consumated overnight.
"We're not saying let's unite tomorrow into some kind of unified government," he told Interfax news agency. "The strengthening of integration connections between our countries is a process."
A top near-term priority is setting up a single currency, the Belarus leader said.
"The main thing is to move towards a unified currency, and the quicker we do this the better," he said. "The Russian president supported this idea today."
Yeltsin said in a state of the nation address to parliament on Thursday that reintegration with Belarus was his top foreign policy priority but it should not be artificially accelerated.

Moscow's renewed wooing of Minsk coincides with a diplomatic offensive against NATO's expansion plans and Western diplomats say talk of effectively shifting Russia's territorial control westward across Belarus may be one of Yeltsin's strongest cards in his strategy to thwart the alliance's plans.
Lukashenko said establishing a common line against NATO expansion was a joint Russian-Belarussian desire, but said unity talks were not directed against the Western alliance.
"This is the first problem which we discussed at length today with the Russian president and Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov," he told Interfax.
"Not once did we say let's move our countries closer together against someone," he said. "We are not setting up our union against anyone."

Briefing reporters after Friday's talks, Yeltsin's adviser on foreign relations, Dmitry Ryurikov, said a bilateral commission overseeing the integration process would meet in Moscow on April 2, the first anniversary of the signing of the "community" pact.
"There are ample grounds for saying that that date will be marked by major new steps in the matter of integration between our two countries," Ryurikov said. He gave no further details.
